_note: FIXTURE, not the real bank. Four questions, one topic, so tests can tell a unit-1-only draw from a units-[1,2] draw by counting. Tiers are spread across the ladder on purpose: unit 1 carries all four, unit 2 carries no 'max', so a test can ask for a tier that has nothing.

questions.q: What is the decimal value of the binary number 1011?
questions.explain: Read the bits by place value from the right: 1x8 + 0x4 + 1x2 + 1x1 = 11. Each position left is worth twice the one before it, which is the whole rule for converting binary to decimal.
why_wrong: 9 is 1001; that drops the 2s bit which 1011 has set.
13 is 1101; the 4s bit is set there and clear in 1011.
15 is 1111, every bit set, which 1011 is not.

questions.q: How many bits are in one byte?
questions.explain: A byte is eight bits, which is why one byte holds 2^8 = 256 distinct values and why a single ASCII character fits in one. Word sizes vary between machines; the byte does not.
why_wrong: Four bits is a nibble, half a byte — it is the unit one hex digit represents.
Sixteen bits is two bytes, often called a half-word.
Thirty-two bits is four bytes, a common word size but not a byte.

questions.q: A colour is written as #FF00AA. Which number system is that, and what is FF in decimal?
questions.explain: Hexadecimal is base 16, with A to F standing for 10 to 15, so FF is 15x16 + 15 = 255. Two hex digits cover exactly one byte, which is why colour channels are written this way.
why_wrong: Octal is base 8 and uses only the digits 0 to 7, so F could not appear in it.
11111111 is the binary form of the same value, but FF itself is written in hex, not binary.
Decimal has no digit F; the letters are what mark this as base 16.

questions.q: You need to store a counter whose largest value is 200. What is the smallest number of bits that will hold it?
questions.explain: n bits hold values 0 to 2^n - 1. Seven bits reach only 127, so they overflow at 200; eight bits reach 255, which is enough. This is the same reason an unsigned byte tops out at 255.
why_wrong: Six bits reach 63, far short of 200.
Seven bits reach 127, so 200 would not fit.
Sixteen bits would hold it, but the question asks for the smallest that works.
